title: Interesting Resources — LLMs 101
body:
## Interesting Resources

A curated collection of resources for learning more about large language models. These are places we've found genuinely useful — not a comprehensive list, just things worth your time.

---

## Foundational Reading

These pieces give you solid grounding in how LLMs actually work.

**[Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)** — The 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. Academic but historically important. You don't need to understand every equation to get the key ideas.

**[The Illustrated Transformer](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/)** — Jay Alammar's visual walkthrough of how Transformers work. One of the best explanations out there for visual learners.

**[What Is ChatGPT Doing… and Why Does It Work?](https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2023/02/what-is-chatgpt-doing-and-why-does-it-work/)** — Stephen Wolfram's detailed explainer. Long but thorough, and doesn't assume much background.

---

## Courses & Interactive Learning

For when you want structured learning rather than scattered reading.

**[fast.ai](https://www.fast.ai/)** — Practical deep learning courses that start from applications and work backwards to theory. Free and well-regarded.

**[Andrej Karpathy's Neural Networks: Zero to Hero](https://karpathy.ai/zero-to-hero.html)** — YouTube series building neural networks from scratch. Requires some coding comfort but explains things clearly.

**[Google's Machine Learning Crash Course](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course)** — Free introductory course covering ML fundamentals. Good starting point before diving into LLM-specific material.

---

## News & Commentary

Staying current without drowning in hype.

**[Simon Willison's Blog](https://simonwillison.net/)** — Practical, technically sharp commentary on LLM developments. Simon writes about what's actually happening with these tools — how they work, what they're good at, where they fail. Good for readers who want depth without wading through academic papers.

**[The Gradient](https://thegradient.pub/)** — Thoughtful long-form pieces about AI research and its implications. More measured than most AI media.

**[Import AI](https://importai.substack.com/)** — Jack Clark's weekly newsletter covering AI research and policy. Dense but informative.

**[One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/)** — Ethan Mollick's Substack focusing on practical applications of AI, especially in education and work.

---

## Model Playgrounds

Places to experiment with models directly.

**[ChatGPT](https://chat.openai.com/)** — OpenAI's conversational interface. Free tier available. The obvious starting point for most people.

**[Claude](https://claude.ai/)** — Anthropic's assistant. Different strengths than ChatGPT — worth comparing responses to the same prompts.

**[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/)** — Hub for open-source models. More technical but lets you try models that aren't behind corporate interfaces.

**[Poe](https://poe.com/)** — Quora's platform for accessing multiple models through one interface. Useful for comparison.

---

*Have a resource suggestion? Let us know what's helped you understand LLMs better.*
